hints: Interpret roots as intersections of \(y=\sec x\) and \(y=2-\tfrac12x\) on \(0\le x<\tfrac\pi2\).
Sketch \(\sec x\) starting at 1 and increasing to its vertical asymptote at \(x=\tfrac\pi2\); sketch the decreasing straight line through \((0,2)\).
Use the opposing monotonic behaviour and the crossing shown by the sketches to justify exactly one intersection.
walkthrough:
Consider the two functions forming the equation $\sec x = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}x$:
$$y_1 = \sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$$
$$y_2 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}x$$

Analyse the behavior and features of $y_1 = \sec x$ on the interval $[0, \dfrac{1}{2}\pi)$:
At $x = 0$, $y_1 = \sec(0) = 1$.
As $x \to \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right)^-$, $\cos x \to 0^+$, so $\sec x \to +\infty$.
The curve $y = \sec x$ is strictly increasing from $(0, 1)$ towards the vertical asymptote at $x = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$.

Analyse the behavior and features of the straight line $y_2 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}x$:
At $x = 0$, $y_2 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(0) = 2$.
At $x = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$, $y_2 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2 - \dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 2 - 0.7854 = 1.2146$.
The line has negative gradient $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and decreases continuously from $(0, 2)$ to $(1.2146)$ at the right boundary.

Compare the two curves across the interval $[0, \dfrac{1}{2}\pi)$:
At $x = 0$, $y_1(0) = 1 < 2 = y_2(0)$, so the line lies above the secant curve.
As $x \to \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$, $y_1(x) \to \infty > 2 - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = y_2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right)$, so the secant curve lies far above the line.
Since $y_1(x)$ is strictly increasing and $y_2(x)$ is strictly decreasing, their graphs must intersect at exactly one point.

Conclude from the sketches:
The sketches of $y = \sec x$ and $y = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}x$ show exactly one point of intersection in $0 \le x < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$, hence the equation has exactly one root in this interval.

hints: Use a continuous difference function, for example \(f(x)=\sec x-2+\tfrac12x\).
Evaluate \(f(0.8)\) and \(f(1)\) in radians, retaining enough figures to see their signs.
Opposite signs at the endpoints, together with continuity and the known uniqueness, locate the root in \((0.8,1)\).
walkthrough:
Define a continuous function $f(x)$ representing the difference between the two sides in radians:
$$f(x) = \sec x - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x} - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x$$

Evaluate $f(x)$ at the lower bound $x = 0.8$ (with calculator in radian mode):
$$\cos(0.8) \approx 0.6967067$$
$$\sec(0.8) = \dfrac{1}{0.6967067} \approx 1.435324$$
$$f(0.8) = 1.435324 - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}(0.8) = 1.435324 - 2 + 0.4 = -0.164676 < 0$$
Alternatively, evaluating each side separately:
$$\sec(0.8) \approx 1.435 < 1.6 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(0.8)$$

Evaluate $f(x)$ at the upper bound $x = 1$ (with calculator in radian mode):
$$\cos(1) \approx 0.5403023$$
$$\sec(1) = \dfrac{1}{0.5403023} \approx 1.8508157$$
$$f(1) = 1.8508157 - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}(1) = 1.8508157 - 2 + 0.5 = +0.350816 > 0$$
Alternatively, evaluating each side separately:
$$\sec(1) \approx 1.851 > 1.5 = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(1)$$

Conclude using the sign change of the continuous function:
Since $f(0.8) \approx -0.165 < 0$ and $f(1) \approx +0.351 > 0$, there is a change of sign between $x = 0.8$ and $x = 1$.
Because $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0.8, 1]$, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, the root of the equation lies between $0.8$ and $1$.

hints: Apply the given fixed-point recurrence in radians, starting from any value in the established interval \((0.8,1)\).
For each step substitute the current \(x_n\) into \(x_{n+1}=\cos^{-1}(2/(4-x_n))\) and record four decimal places.
Continue until the iterates stabilise sufficiently to justify a unique value when rounded to two decimal places.
walkthrough:
State the iterative formula, working throughout in radians:
$$x_{n+1} = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2}{4 - x_n}\right)$$

Choose an initial value in the interval $(0.8, 1)$, for example $x_1 = 0.9$:
For $n = 1$:
$$4 - x_1 = 4 - 0.9 = 3.1$$
$$\dfrac{2}{4 - x_1} = \dfrac{2}{3.1} \approx 0.6451613$$
$$x_2 = \cos^{-1}(0.6451613) \approx 0.869186 \implies x_2 = 0.8692$$

Verify convergence to 2 decimal places:
Both $x_5 = 0.8762$ and $x_6 = 0.8760$ round to $0.88$ to 2 decimal places.
We can also verify the root in the interval $(0.875, 0.885)$:
$$f(0.875) = \sec(0.875) - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}(0.875) \approx 1.56066 - 2 + 0.4375 = -0.00184 < 0$$
$$f(0.885) = \sec(0.885) - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}(0.885) \approx 1.58334 - 2 + 0.4425 = +0.02584 > 0$$
The sign change in $(0.875, 0.885)$ confirms that to 2 decimal places:
$$x = 0.88$$
